Ford Ranger Super Duty Hy-Rail Conversion Reports for Railway Work
15 photos
Photo: Ford
The Ranger Super Duty has already undertaken plenty of jobs that would overwhelm a regular mid-size pickup. Its latest conversion, however, ups the ante to railway work. Together with Ford Pro's Convertor division, Australian specialist Aries Rail has developed a hy-rail system that lets the diesel-powered truck drive along railway tracks.
Ford engineers helped Aries integrate the hardware into the chassis, and the Dearborn-based automaker further made a bunch of modifications to the SYNC infotainment system for this application. Aries Rail spent four decades doing such conversions with a bunch of different vehicles, but the Ranger Super Duty program is on another level altogether.
Railway operators use road-rail vehicles to inspect tracks, clear obstacles, and send maintenance crews to sections where ordinary automobiles cannot reach. Aries Rail's solution starts with a quartet of flanged steel guide wheels that are raised or lowered hydraulically.
Joining the 70-series Toyota Land Cruiser hy-rail conversion, the Ranger Super Duty program gives Aries Rail another platform to work with. The heavy-duty axles, thicker driveshafts, upgraded suspension, and reinforced chassis all recommended the Ranger Super Duty for this job, and Aries Rail wanted to exploit all of those attributes without compromising the underlying vehicle's usability.
The collab started in 2025, with Ford Pro Converter providing the engineering support. Under this program, approved converters receive the mounting manual that explains how to work with the Ranger Super Duty's structure and mounting points. Aries Rail also used computer-aided design data to develop a unique installation rather than adapt an existing rail system for the Ranger Super Duty.
Photo: Ford Ford helped Aries optimize the mounting and installation, and Ford's involvement in the project avoided compromising the vehicle's warranty. The cabin required just as much attention, and this brings us to a company dubbed Opses.
The technology partner came up with an integrated solution for the Ranger Super Duty hy-rail conversion, routing the controls for the hydraulic rail guidance system through the SYNC infotainment display instead of adding another display or switch panel. Aries had never integrated the rail guidance controls this way before.
A standardized conversion process allows Aries to build the same configuration over and over again at its facilities around Australia, which makes the conversion particularly relevant to commercial customers. A fleet operator needs consistency across the board, and having an identical conversion process makes everything easier on both sides.
Ariel Rail sees opportunities beyond the Australian market, with chief executive officer Nathan Bender claiming that said conversion could eventually become a global product. Neither Aries nor Ford announced international sales plans or specific export markets. For the time being, the demo vehicle will have to suffice at the AusRAIL 2026 in Brisbane, which runs through November 25, 2026.
The steel wheels are there only for guidance, which means the rubber wheels and V6 diesel engine do the heavy lifting on railroad tracks. Similar to the standard Ranger Super Duty, the 3.0-liter unit is connected to a 10-speed auto box and produces 154 kW (207 hp) at full chatter. Its peak torque is estimated at 600 Newton-meters, a figure that can be read as 443 pound-feet in the US market where Ford doesn't sell this fellow.
